item.title: J Street’s Super PAC Targets Two Republicans Backed by AIPAC
item.description:
The super PAC for J Street, a liberal pro-Israel advocacy group, released two ads on Tuesday targeting a pair of Republican members of Congress who have been endorsed by AIPAC.

The ads are the first time J Street’s super PAC has taken on the American Israel Public Affairs Committee in a general election, which has long prided itself on bipartisanship and backed members from both parties. But AIPAC has increasingly become a pariah in some Democratic circles and has faced a backlash after spending millions in Democratic primaries.

One ad criticizes Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa’s First Congressional District and the other denounces Ryan Mackenzie in Pennsylvania’s Seventh Congressional District for their positions on health care and ties to insurance companies.

J Street, which refers to itself as “pro-Israel and pro-peace,” has sought to position itself as an influential player in Democratic politics and on Capitol Hill. The group’s super PAC, J Street Action Fund, has spent $3 million in the midterm campaign. That is a record for J Street, but it is a small fraction of the tens of millions spent by AIPAC’s super PAC, United Democracy Project.

Neither of the new ads explicitly mentions Israel, which organizers say is not the primary issue for the overwhelming majority of voters.

J Street Action Fund this month also released an ad condemning the Republican Senate candidate in Georgia, Mike Collins, for his reported history of hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views.

“J Street Action Fund’s investment in these targeted races represents the views of a majority of Jewish Americans who understand that we need to preserve American democracy and fight xenophobia in all its forms to keep our communities safe,” Tali DeGroot, the group’s political director, said in a statement.

item.title: Trump Invokes Antisemitic Trope Again at Rally for Kansas Senator
item.description:
President Trump invoked a centuries-old antisemitic trope to defend the aggressive debt-collecting tactics of Senator Roger Marshall, the first-term Republican fighting for re-election in Kansas, before the senator began his political career.

At a rally on Monday with Mr. Marshall in Park City, Kan., the president said Mr. Marshall’s opponents had unfairly cast him as “some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” an apparent reference to recent reporting by The New York Times that revealed that Mr. Marshall had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding medical bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist. Mr. Marshall, The Times reported, routinely charged an 18 percent annual interest rate and also garnished patients’ paychecks and bank accounts. Mr. Trump did not mention The Times by name.

Shylock is the name of the Jewish moneylender from Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice.” The character, who demands a pound of human flesh as collateral for a loan, has become shorthand for antisemitic representations of avarice and usury.

At the rally, Mr. Trump sought to make the case that Mr. Marshall had been following the law.

“He’s a fine person,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Marshall, who is not Jewish. “And he was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request, strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people. And they made it like, ‘Oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy.’”

Doctors have wide discretion on how to handle unpaid bills and are not required by law to sue patients or involve debt collectors.

“The term ‘Shylock’ is rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype,” the Anti-Defamation League wrote Tuesday on social media, after The Times reached out to the Jewish advocacy group for comment on Mr. Trump’s remarks. “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community.”

It was not the first time Mr. Trump has used the term publicly. During a rally last year in Iowa, he said that farmers should not have to go to, “in some cases, Shylocks and bad people” to borrow money. Afterward, Mr. Trump said he didn’t know it was an antisemitic slur.

“You view it differently than me,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the time. “I’ve never heard that.”

Jewish leaders and lawmakers last year quickly denounced his use of the term. The Anti-Defamation League called the trope “extremely offensive and dangerous.” Representative Jerry Nadler, Democrat of New York, said it was “one of the most recognizable antisemitic slurs in the English language.”

The Senate race in Kansas, which Republican leaders did not view as competitive just a few months ago, has evolved into one of the tightest contests of the midterm elections. Mr. Marshall faces Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who is vying to become the first Democrat from Kansas elected to the Senate since 1932.

During the campaign, Mr. Hamilton has turned Mr. Marshall’s debt-collecting practices into fodder for political attacks and advertisements, one of which shows a former patient of Mr. Marshall’s saying she had been arrested while eight months pregnant for a $50 missed payment. Lawyers for Mr. Marshall called the ad “defamatory,” though Mr. Hamilton’s campaign continued to use it.

Other politicians have faced criticism for using the term “Shylock” in the past. In 2014, then-Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. apologized after he said it during a speech.

Mr. Trump’s comments come at a time when Republicans up and down the ballot, and across the country, have been trying to win over Jewish voters who feel disillusioned by the Democratic Party’s posture toward Israel. Republican leaders have seized on opportunities to draw a contrast on issues relating to Israel and antisemitism, often casting their Democratic opponents as threatening. Republican leaders have been relentless in their use of Islamophobic attacks against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, who is Muslim. Mr. Trump recently claimed that the candidate “hates Jews,” to which Dr. El-Sayed responded, “I love and revere Judaism and the Jewish people.”

Republican Senate candidates across the Midwest have struggled to make their case to voters amid rising energy prices and Mr. Trump’s unpopular war in Iran. Some, like Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa and former Representative Mike Rogers in Michigan, have sought to distance themselves from the president on these issues. Mr. Marshall has not.

For years, Mr. Trump and his campaign have been accused of stealthily trying to win over racists and antisemites, a claim they reject. In 2016, Mr. Trump, then the presumptive Republican presidential nominee, posted an image on Twitter depicting Hillary Clinton beside a Jewish star and piles of money that had previously appeared on a message board known for antisemitism and white supremacy.

During Mr. Trump’s second term, official government social media accounts, including those for the White House, have made dozens of posts that invoke white supremacist and neo-Nazi messaging, drawing condemnation from Jewish leaders and experts in online extremism.

item.title: Attack Ad Featuring Candidate’s Mother Turns Ohio Governor’s Race Even Uglier
item.description:
A new attack ad in the Ohio governor's race features the mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton — estranged from her daughter over allegations of molestation by a stepfather — calling the candidate a liar.

Republicans hailed the ad, which began circulating on social media Monday night, as a bombshell, while Democrats called it a new low by Dr. Acton’s opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, in a campaign that was already one of the nation’s ugliest. Dr. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, condemned it as “a despicable low.”

Donna Arthur, Dr. Acton’s mother, says in the ad, “Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself.”

On the campaign trail and during her time as the director of the Ohio Department of Health, Dr. Acton has shared details of a troubled childhood in which she was homeless for a time and was molested by her stepfather.

In 2019, Dr. Acton gave an interview to The Vindicator, the since-folded daily newspaper of Youngstown, Ohio, in which she disclosed being sexually abused between the ages of 9 and 12. In 1978, after her biological father made a report to the police, her stepfather was charged with rape and indicted by a grand jury. He pleaded not guilty.

In 2020, Ms. Arthur came forward to a conservative website to say her daughter’s claims of homelessness were exaggerated. Ms. Arthur shared that after her husband was arrested, Dr. Acton testified against him in court. Ms. Arthur supported her husband, rather than her daughter.

In the new ad, Ms. Arthur does not refer to the allegations of molestation. Instead, she dismisses Dr. Acton’s story that she lived in a tent as a child.

Both women have said that they have not seen or spoken to each other since that day in court in 1978.

Mr. Stearns, Dr. Acton’s brother, said in a statement Tuesday that he and his sister were removed from their mother’s custody after the arrest.

“Our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died,” Mr. Stearns said. “This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to substantive questions about the ad, including whether Ms. Arthur was paid to participate. And it is unclear if the ad came from Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign or another organization that is backing his race.

But on Tuesday afternoon, amid a considerable backlash, Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign appeared to endorse it.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth,” Connie Luck, a spokeswoman for the Ramaswamy campaign, said in the statement.

Though the spot has gained traction on social media, including in an X post from Donald Trump Jr., it has not yet appeared on Ohio television, according to AdImpact.

Democrats have attacked Mr. Ramaswamy for a separate ad that a political website pointed out shows a man convicted of child sexual abuse. The spot was focused on a woman named Patty, who was nearly in tears over increases in property taxes and said she was afraid that she would lose her home. It showed Mr. Ramaswamy meeting Patty at a county fair, while her husband stood beside her.

Last week, The Bulwark reported that her husband was Vernon Edwards, a registered sex offender convicted in 2006 of “gross sexual imposition” with a victim under the age of 13.

Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign later said it removed clips of Mr. Edwards from the ad, but according to AdImpact, the ad is still running unchanged.

Family members, such as President Trump’s niece Mary Trump, the siblings of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the siblings of Representative Paul Gosar, Republican of Arizona, have stepped forward in past campaigns to oppose their kin.

But few cases have been so visceral as the anti-Acton ad. Republicans had already attacked Dr. Acton in starkly personal terms, presenting her as a violent drunk, inflating the events of a single night in the Columbus, Ohio, suburbs in late August 2019 when police were dispatched to Dr. Acton’s house, but no charges were filed.

The Acton campaign has presented Mr. Ramaswamy as a con man and out-of-touch billionaire.

Whether yet another attack ad will have a meaningful impact on the race is unclear, said Melissa K. Miller, a Bowling Green State University professor who has been closely watching the race. This late in October, she said, voters are quick to tune out the endless political commercials on their televisions, and many have already made up their mind about who they want to be their next governor.

Campbell Robertson contributed reporting.

item.title: Richard Riehle, Prolific Actor Who Appeared in ‘Office Space,’ Dies at 78
item.description:
Richard Riehle, a prolific character actor best known for playing an anxious product manager in the 1999 film “Office Space,” died on Thursday. He was 78.

His representatives provided no other details about his death.

In a career that included more than 400 credits over several decades, Mr. Riehle performed in films, theater, television series, mini-series and even video games.

But Mr. Riehle was most likely best known for playing Tom Smykowski in “Office Space,” the cult classic and satire directed by Mike Judge about corporate employees being victimized by meaningless metrics, efficiency experts and other management fads.

Mr. Riehle’s character, Tom, is extremely anxious, terrified of losing his job at Initech, a tech company — which he eventually does. When corporate efficiency consultants interrogate Tom about what he does all day, he says:

Well — well look. I already told you: I deal with the goddamn customers so the engineers don’t have to. I have people skills; I am good at dealing with people. Can’t you understand that? What the hell is wrong with you people?

Tom later gets into a hit-and-run accident, leaving him in a full-body cast and wheelchair. After he receives a hefty settlement, he no longer needs to work.

Instead, he pursues his dream of creating a “Jump to Conclusions” floor mat, with squares with different conclusions that people can, literally, jump to.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

“This is a horrible idea,” one of his colleagues tells him.

Richard Riehle was born on May 12, 1948 in Menomonee Falls, Wis. His father, Herbert John Riehle, was an assistant postmaster, and his mother, Mary Margaret, was a nurse. His father died when he was 13.

As the oldest of six children, Mr. Riehle worked 40 hours a week at a grocery store to help support his family.

He participated in high school plays, but after graduation he entered a seminary to become a priest. After getting caught sneaking back to the seminary from seeing “Lawrence of Arabia” without permission, he decided that the priesthood was not for him.

“They sat me down at that point and just asked me if I really thought this was the right place for me,” he told Notre Dame Magazine in 2011. “We both knew the answer.”

Mr. Riehle attended the University of Notre Dame, where he acted, directed and built sets. He became fluent in German during a study abroad program in Austria.

After graduating from Notre Dame in 1970, he became a teaching assistant at the University of Minnesota, where he earned a master’s degree in fine arts and began his professional stage career, spending years working in regional theater. He also took on small screen roles.

“I was content during that time,” Mr. Riehle told his alumni magazine. “I always seemed to find work.”

He made his debut on Broadway in “Execution of Justice” in 1986, and stayed in New York for another decade, later appearing in “The Iceman Cometh” in 1999, alongside Paul Giamatti. He appeared in dozens of TV shows, including “Hot Pursuit,” “L.A. Law,” “Quantum Leap,” “Murder, She Wrote” and “The West Wing.”

He even appeared in the soap opera “One Life to Live,” and played a high school principal in a TV adaptation of “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.”

“I always wanted the role that would bring something out of me, force me to find something extra,” Mr. Riehle told his alumni magazine. “The lead isn’t always the best part in a play or a movie.”

His breakthrough in film occurred in 1989, when he played a bureaucratic quartermaster in the Civil War drama “Glory.” Roles in more than 100 films followed, including the “The Fugitive,” “Casino,” and playing parts in three “Star Trek” franchises.

“Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity,” his talent agency, Artists & Representatives, and management company, Wright Entertainment, said in a joint statement.

Complete information on survivors was not immediately available.

Mr. Riehle has parts in approximately another dozen films that are in production, or that have been completed.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Man Who Took Flamingo From Las Vegas Hotel Is Found Guilty of Cruelty
item.description:
It started as a work trip to Las Vegas in March. So how did a man end up shirtless in a hotel carrying a flamingo by the neck? One possible reason was the 30 to 40 beers he drank.

The man, Mitchell G. Fairbarn of Ontario, was convicted on Monday of stealing a flamingo from its habitat at a Las Vegas hotel and taking it back to his room. A jury in Clark County, Nev., found Mr. Fairbarn guilty of one felony charge and one misdemeanor charge of cruelty to animals. Sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 1.

The police said that Mr. Fairbarn, who was 33 when he committed the crime, went into the wildlife habitat on the grounds of the Flamingo Hotel Las Vegas, grabbed a flamingo named Peachy by its neck and legs, wrapped the bird in a shirt and jacket and took it to his room on the 14th floor, according to an arrest report.

Video reviewed by the police and cited in the initial report showed that Mr. Fairbarn grabbed one bird by the legs, took a picture with his cellphone, then waded into the water in a hunt for a second bird, grabbing one by the neck.

Mr. Fairbarn took that bird, Peachy, into the hotel, footage shows. Surveillance photos show him shirtless in a hotel elevator and in a hall with the flamingo.

The resort said that three birds in total were injured in the episode.

Mr. Fairbarn is self-employed as a civil contractor and had no prior criminal history, according to court documents.

According to the police report, Mr. Fairbarn said that he had been trying to help a bird that he saw in distress. Mr. Fairbarn “admitted to his actions being repulsive,” the report said. He told them that he thought he was being helpful by fixing a bird’s wing, but said he was drunk and did not remember chasing after the birds.

Photos and videos on Mr. Fairbarn’s phone show him laughing and saying, “I’m taking it home,” as he walked the bird back to his room, the police said.

“I thought it would be, at the time, funny,” he testified in court.

He also testified that before the jaunt with the birds he had consumed 30 to 40 beers, local news media reported. He acknowledged at trial that the video “doesn’t look good.”

Caesars, which owns the hotel, said in a statement: “We are grateful this matter was taken seriously and appreciate the work of law enforcement, prosecutors and the animal care professionals who responded. This was a deeply upsetting incident, and our focus remains on the care and well-being of the animals at the Flamingo Wildlife Habitat.”

Caesars said on Tuesday that Peachy was “doing well, and we are grateful that he continues to receive attentive care from our dedicated animal care team.”

Mr. Fairbarn said in court that after his arrest was made public he had received death threats and changed his children’s schools in Canada. He has been under house arrest in Las Vegas.

A lawyer for Mr. Fairbarn did not respond to a request for comment.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” his lawyer, Josh Tomsheck, said in court, according to The Associated Press. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”

The wildlife habitat at the Flamingo Hotel includes a flock of Chilean flamingos, exotic waterfowl, brown pelicans, hummingbirds and fish, according to the hotel’s website.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: If Democrats Win Congress, Could the G.O.P. Refuse to Seat Them?
item.description:
President Trump’s unfounded claims of large-scale voter fraud have Democrats bracing for what they worry could be substantial interference by the federal government in the midterm elections.

But with polls showing that Democrats are likely to win control of the House, some lawmakers and commentators have turned their attention to a different scenario that could unfold after the voting: Republicans in Congress, egged on by Mr. Trump, could try to block them from assuming the majority by refusing to seat elected Democrats.

The possibility sounds far-fetched and is regarded by many legal scholars as a vanishingly remote one.

“It requires a lot of ducks to be in a row that I don’t think would be in a row,” said Brian C. Kalt, a law professor at Michigan State University.

But the same might have been said in 2020 of the possibility that Republican lawmakers, under pressure from Mr. Trump, would challenge the Electoral College results that confirmed Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory. That is precisely what a majority of Republicans voted to do on Jan. 6, 2021, an effort in which Representative Mike Johnson, who has since become speaker, played a major role.

That is among the reasons that two moderate House members, one from each party, have asked their colleagues to pledge to accept certified election results and block efforts to refuse or delay seating winners.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said this month that his party was “preparing for all eventualities, including making sure that the results of the American people that emerge from the Nov. 3 general election are brought to life on Jan. 3 in the new Congress.”

That is the day that the next Congress is scheduled to convene. Here’s a closer look at what could happen.

The Constitution gives states the authority to administer their elections, and each one sends certificates of election verifying the winners to the House and Senate.

For decades, those certifications were part of a largely routine process, but since the 2020 election, a small number of state officials have voted against certifying elections or threatened to refuse to do so. Those efforts have been unsuccessful but at times have required other officials and courts to intervene.

Some federal election experts believe that this could be the greatest pressure point for efforts to reverse or sow doubt about the midterm election results. Democrats have said they are concerned that Mr. Trump has promoted false claims about election integrity to lay the groundwork for challenges to the counting, canvassing and certification of ballots.

If races are not certified, seats could remain unfilled when the new Congress first meets, which could affect the balance of power in the House. In 2021, a seat in upstate New York was left vacant for more than a month as an election dispute played out in court.

Because every House seat is up for election every two years, newly elected representatives must be sworn in at the start of the new Congress. The outgoing House of Representatives — and the majority in control of it — ceases to exist at noon on Jan. 3, and the chamber has to reconstitute itself.

In the interim, while nobody is in charge, federal law gives the clerk of the House, the chamber’s chief administrative official who is chosen by the speaker and then elected, the duty of assembling the list of new members. The statute directs the clerk to include only people “whose credentials show that they were regularly elected in accordance” with state and federal law.

The current clerk is Kevin F. McCumber.

Most election law experts believe this is essentially a bookkeeping task in which the clerk is required to recognize valid certificates of election that have been sent by the states. Professor Kalt said that clerks traditionally make sure that “the paperwork is right” but do not evaluate how an election was called or conducted.

“There’s not a lot of judgment happening here,” he said. “They’re just saying, ‘OK, the rules were followed. This person was elected. This person is on the roll of the members-elect.’”

But some commentators have speculated that Republicans could seek to intervene by pressuring the clerk to refuse to recognize Democratic winners — as Mr. Trump leaned on Vice President Mike Pence to do in 2021 — or seek to replace him with someone who would.

Such an action would likely prompt legal challenges, and many election law experts believe the courts would intervene.

But some Democrats note that Mr. Johnson has in the past resorted to extraordinary measures to bar a member of their party from being seated in the House, as he did when he delayed for nearly two months last year before swearing in Representative Adelita Grijalva of Arizona. (Mr. Johnson said he had done so because the House was not in session, though there is no rule barring the seating of a member during such a period.)

While states control their elections, the Constitution also says that each house of Congress “shall be the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members.”

The new Congress — not the outgoing one — is responsible for settling contested races.

The House has faced hundreds of contested elections over its history, and Congress passed a law in the 1960s, the Federal Contested Elections Act, that establishes a procedure for doing so. (The law does not address the Senate.)

After a winner has been declared, the losing candidate has 30 days to contest the result with the House clerk. The burden is on challengers to prove that the results “entitle” them to the seat.

The House Administration Committee adjudicates contested elections. It can conduct an investigation and make a recommendation to the full House on which candidate to swear in.

Derek T. Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said that members whose elections were certified had often been seated provisionally while their contests were being adjudicated.

“If somebody shows up to Congress with a certificate saying, ‘I am the member who’s been elected from this district,’ they still get seated,” he said.

In 2021, Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an Iowa Republican, came to the Capitol after a recount showed she had just won her race by six votes. The Democratic candidate, Rita Hart, had filed a contest, but Ms. Miller-Meeks was allowed to take her seat while the committee investigated. Ultimately, Ms. Hart withdrew her challenge.

There’s another way that elections can be challenged in the House. After a speaker is selected and sworn in, any member-elect can challenge the right of another representative-elect to be sworn in.

Under the House’s precedents, the person being challenged is asked to step aside while the rest of the members take their oaths of office. After that, the lawmakers vote on whether to swear in those who were asked to step aside, or they can refer the question of seating them for investigation to the Administration Committee.

This avenue has been used less frequently since the Federal Contested Elections Act was enacted. But in 2021, Representative-elect Chip Roy, Republican of Texas, challenged the seating of 67 members-elect from the battleground states where Mr. Trump focused his false claims of voter fraud in the 2020 election.

Mr. Roy, who later voted against Mr. Trump’s efforts to overturn his election loss, appeared to be trying to make a point by arguing that Republicans who questioned the presidential results should be willing to lodge similar objections in House races in the same states.

But Democrats immediately brought a vote on whether to swear in the 67 members-elect, and it passed overwhelmingly, with just two Republicans, neither of them Mr. Roy, opposing it.

Notably, the disputed members-elect from those six states were allowed to vote on whether they could be seated.

The last time the House refused on the first day of a new Congress to seat a member whose victory was certified was in 1985.

Democrats — who already held a large majority — objected to seating a Republican from a hotly contested district in Indiana, citing issues with vote counting and the certification process that they contended needed to be investigated.

Voting mostly along partisan lines, the House left the seat vacant and referred the issue to the administration panel. A task force led by Democrats oversaw its own recount and after four months concluded that the Democratic candidate had won by just four votes. The House gave him the seat.

In the Senate, where only a third of senators are up for election every two years, federal law requires states to send certificates of election to the vice president, who is the president of the Senate.

Unlike in the House, no federal statute governs how the list of new senators is compiled. The Senate’s rules put the secretary of the Senate in charge of compiling the certificates of election, but they do not make clear whether and on what grounds the secretary or vice president can reject them.

The Senate has dealt less frequently with election disputes in recent history, in part because statewide elections tend to have larger voting margins. It has fewer established procedures and has tended to operate on precedents when considering contested elections.

As in the House, the new Senate adjudicates election disputes, and challenges are usually referred to the Rules Committee while the senator-elect in question is seated “without prejudice.” If the investigation finds in favor of the challenger, the seated senator could then be removed from the Senate by a simple majority vote rather than the two-thirds majority typically required to expel a senator.

In 1997, the Senate provisionally seated Senator Mary Landrieu, Democrat of Louisiana, while the Rules Committee investigated accusations of voter fraud in her state. After months of investigating, the committee found in her favor.

The Senate has also left seats vacant while election disputes were being fought. Senator Al Franken, Democrat of Minnesota, was not sworn in until seven months after his 2008 election, after a long recount and court battle.

But a Senate race in New Hampshire in 1974 made Mr. Franken’s path look easy. In the Election Day vote, the Republican, Louis C. Wyman, won by 355 votes. After a recount, the Democrat, John A. Durkin, was ahead by 10. After another recount, Mr. Wyman was ahead by two votes and was certified the winner.

Mr. Durkin asked the Senate to review the election, but the Rules Committee deadlocked and asked the full Senate to vote.

Instead, the Senate sent the disputed election back to the panel, which spent months reviewing 3,500 disputed ballots that it had shipped from New Hampshire. Still, senators were deadlocked on several issues that would have swayed the outcome, so the committee sent the full Senate a list of 35 disputes.

After six weeks of debate, senators had resolved just one of them. With lawmakers set to leave for their August recess and no clear end in sight, both Mr. Wyman and Mr. Durkin agreed to a new election, and the Senate declared the seat vacant.

Mr. Durkin ultimately won.

item.title: Alabama Man’s Death Sentence Is Commuted as Governor Cites Thin Evidence
item.description:
Gov. Kay Ivey of Alabama on Tuesday commuted the death sentence of a 53-year-old man convicted in the 1995 killing of a sheriff’s deputy, citing “not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment.”

It is the third time that Ms. Ivey, a Republican, has commuted the death sentence of a prisoner. Alabama has executed 27 prisoners since she became governor in 2017.

The man whose death sentence was commuted on Tuesday, Toforest Johnson, was convicted of capital murder in 1998 in connection with the killing of William G. Hardy, a deputy in Jefferson County, Ala., who was fatally shot while working a security job at a Birmingham hotel.

Mr. Johnson has maintained his innocence. He said he was at a nightclub on the night of the shooting in July 1995.

Mr. Johnson’s conviction largely relied on the testimony of a woman, Violet Ellison, who said during his trial that she had heard him confess to the crime during a three-way phone call. Ms. Ellison received a $5,000 reward from the state for her help. That information was not initially disclosed and was revealed to Mr. Johnson’s lawyers two decades later. His lawyers also noted that no physical evidence had ever linked him to the crime.

Mr. Johnson’s lawyers say jurors never heard from witnesses who could have corroborated his whereabouts during the crime.

Ms. Ivey said Mr. Johnson would be sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

“My decision is not a determination of innocence,” Ms. Ivey said, “but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence.”

Ms. Ivey’s decision came weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, which renewed debates about the effectiveness of lethal injections and about capital punishment.

Mr. Johnson’s case gained national attention after becoming the subject of a popular podcast released in 2023. Danny Carr, the district attorney in Jefferson County, helped spur a re-examination of the case in 2020 when he voiced concerns about the prosecution and asked for a new trial.

Steve Marshall, the attorney general of Alabama, declined to consider the request. Lawyers in the attorney general’s office wrote in 2022 that “Mr. Carr’s opinion that Johnson should receive a new trial is just that, his opinion.”

In 2024, Mr. Carr released the findings of a post-conviction review, which found several flaws in the investigation and prosecution of Mr. Johnson. For instance, credible witnesses placed Mr. Johnson elsewhere at the time of the killing, the review found, and Mr. Johnson had said he was at Tee’s Place, a nightclub across town.

In 2014, Jeff Wallace, who was the lead prosecutor in Mr. Johnson’s case, acknowledged in a court hearing that the case against Mr. Johnson was “not very strong because it depended on the testimony of Violet Ellison,” records show. Six years later, Mr. Wallace announced his support for a new trial for Mr. Johnson.

Ms. Ellison had also served as a key witness for the state in other criminal cases around the same time that Mr. Johnson’s case was pending. One resulted in an acquittal, and the other was dismissed before trial.

“A thorough review and investigation of the entire case leaves no confidence in the integrity of Johnson’s conviction,” Mr. Carr wrote in a 2024 brief expressing his support for a new trial, noting that “the interest of justice” demanded it.

“The foundation of this conviction has disintegrated,” he added.

Ty Alper, one of Mr. Johnson’s lawyers, said in a statement Tuesday that his team was “grateful to Governor Ivey for diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution.”

Since the 1970s, more than 75 people have been executed in Alabama, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which collects data on executions. Only a handful of states have had more executions in that time, including Oklahoma, Texas and Missouri.

Mr. Alper said it was up to the courts to overturn Mr. Johnson’s conviction and grant him a new trial. His case is now pending in a county court.

“We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” he said.

item.title: Republican Women Lean on Working Mom Cred to Stump in Tight Iowa Race
item.description:
Representative Ashley Hinson, Iowa’s Republican nominee for Senate, was about to run an errand this month when her minivan’s console announced a phone call from “DJT.” She answered to hear President Trump say, “Ashley, it’s your favorite president.”

He asked how Ms. Hinson was feeling about the polls, she recalled — a reflection of deep Republican concern regarding a conservative-leaning state whose Senate race has turned into a tossup amid growing voter dissatisfaction with Mr. Trump. Ms. Hinson recounted the call Tuesday at a Des Moines campaign event with Senator Katie Britt of Alabama, who was in town to try to shore up support from Republican voters.

With Mr. Trump’s low approval rating dragging down Republican prospects nationwide, the party has flooded Iowa with advertising to help Ms. Hinson regain ground against Josh Turek, a state representative and the Democratic nominee for Senate. A parade of national Republican officials have also visited in recent weeks. Mr. Trump will be in Sioux City on Thursday in an attempt to juice turnout in one of the state’s reddest enclaves.

The story about the call from Mr. Trump also served to highlight an identity that Ms. Hinson has emphasized on the campaign trail: working mother. She had just dropped her sons off at school, she said, when the president called. She and Ms. Britt share the distinction of being among the few women in Congress with school-age children. Ms. Britt, who was elected in 2022, said she turned to Ms. Hinson for guidance on adapting to life in Washington.

“I missed my husband. I missed my kids,” Ms. Britt said, and then added, “Learning from Ashley and sitting down with Ashley is what actually made the difference for me.”

Ms. Britt, 44, said she “cannot wait” for Ms. Hinson, who is 43, to replace her as the youngest female senator. In Congress today, “you’ve got a lot of social media stars, not a lot of statesmen,” Ms. Britt said. “This woman is a statesman.”

Instead of a focus on transgender athletes and the other red-meat social issues that have animated campaign appearances by Mr. Trump, Vice President JD Vance and many other Republican leaders, Ms. Hinson and Ms. Britt largely skirted culture-war topics.

They talked about efforts to keep children away from screens, about Ms. Hinson’s work to expand over-the-counter access to contraceptives and about Ms. Britt’s hope to make in vitro fertilization more affordable. Ms. Hinson also talked about rural Iowa health facilities getting grants from Mr. Trump’s sweeping tax reduction and spending bill.

She did not mention the legislation’s broad restrictions on Medicaid, which have forced some hospitals to limit their services.

Near the end of the event, she reminded her audience to keep up with their routine checkups. “Ladies, get your mammograms!”

item.title: Trump Pushes to Evict the Press From the White House
item.description:
In late August, during one of Karoline Leavitt’s final meetings with President Trump in the Oval Office, he pitched her on an idea in front of several senior aides. He told her to move reporters out of the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, which would effectively remove news organizations from the White House. It would be, he told her, her “last legacy.”

But the proposal never moved forward while she was there. The president had put the request to her several times over months, according to three people with knowledge of the discussions who were not authorized to speak publicly. Ms. Leavitt officially stepped down as White House press secretary on Aug. 27.

Mr. Trump has told aides he would prefer to bring back the indoor pool President Franklin D. Roosevelt added in 1933 as therapy for his polio-afflicted legs; President Richard Nixon later covered it over to make room for the news media. Journalists who are credentialed to cover the White House work out of a small office space connected to the press briefing room.

While moving the media out of the White House may be a relatively small debate considering Mr. Trump’s attacks on journalists more broadly, it would be highly symbolic. The proximity of the media to the seat of U.S. executive power has long been an acknowledgment of the importance of a free press in a constitutional democracy.

It would also be a decision that would be difficult to undo by future presidents.

Mr. Trump has brought up the press-eviction idea before, dating to his first term, and he has never quite dropped it. A growing number of people around him favor the idea. Several close to him believe that moving the news media, most likely to the Eisenhower Executive Office Building across the street, may be the latest escalation in a remarkable series of moves against the news media that have already gone further than most of them expected.

As recently as Sept. 27, Mr. Trump shared a pair of images on Truth Social showing the briefing room as it is now, captioned “Fake News,” alongside another that shows the space reimagined as a gilded swimming pool, captioned “FDR Pool.”

The Wall Street Journal reported last month that Mr. Trump had repeatedly discussed moving the press corps out of the White House, and that his advisers had so far either offered pushback or waited for him to move on.

What has changed since Mr. Trump’s first term or even earlier this term is the staff around him. The president’s core team has shrunk from the already-tight unit that he brought into the White House last year. During earlier discussions, most of Mr. Trump’s senior aides agreed it served him better to keep the media nearby. But Mr. Trump has grown more enraged about his press coverage, and other advisers of growing influence have encouraged him to take drastic measures to punish journalists.

“America is rightly distrustful of the fake news media because they fabricate stories based off lies and sources who are not even privy to any type of information,” said Steven Cheung, the White House communications director. “All options remain on the table, and we will make an announcement when appropriate.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

During the 2016 Trump transition, Stephen K. Bannon, then the incoming chief strategist, suggested moving the press corps out of the West Wing, to a townhouse near Lafayette Square. Senior officials rejected the idea out of hand. Mr. Bannon proposed the Eisenhower building as a fallback option.

In January 2017, the incoming chief of staff, Reince Priebus, publicly confirmed that the team was weighing a move of press briefings to that location, framing it as a way to accommodate more reporters. But he and others dropped the idea, ultimately viewing it as too disruptive and impractical.

“From the moment I arrived in the White House I believed it was a national security threat to have the press literally surround the Oval Office — and devised a plan to either move them off campus next to the Blair House or at least to E.O.B.,” Mr. Bannon recalled in a statement to The New York Times this month. “But definitely physically remove them from the West Wing. That plan landed with a thud among all the other senior advisers to the president.”

The idea came up again during the summer of 2017, when the West Wing was undergoing renovations. A former administration official recalled that it was less a formal plan than an impulse tied to the renovations: With the space torn up anyway, why let the reporters back in? The official said that Sean Spicer, the departing press secretary, and Sarah Huckabee Sanders, his successor, questioned the logistical complexities. It soon died again.

The idea came up yet again during the presidential transition in late 2024. Most of Mr. Trump’s advisers thought it was better to leave the news media inside the White House. They knew Mr. Trump liked to call the cameras into the Oval Office at a moment’s notice. And several of his more seasoned advisers suspected that if they followed his direction to evict the press — and his coverage got worse — Mr. Trump would blame them for the inevitable results of his own idea.

But even without physically moving the news media to a building outside the White House main gates, the administration has for months been building up a buffer against the press. Last fall, Mr. Trump’s team barred reporters from entering “Upper Press,” the area near the press secretary’s office, without an appointment.

It has been more than 30 years since another president seriously considered removing the news media from the White House. President Bill Clinton’s first communications director, George Stephanopoulos, recounted in his memoir that in 1993 the first lady, Hillary Clinton, wanted to convert the press quarters back into a swimming pool. When word of her plan leaked, the blowback quickly ended it.

But Mr. Trump currently faces no comparable pressure to accommodate a news media that is despised by so many of his supporters. He has received relatively little backlash so far — even from Democrats — against his anti-media moves.

Mr. Trump entered his second term emboldened by his victory, and he quickly went on offense against media companies that had covered him critically. He filed lawsuits against ABC, CBS and The Des Moines Register. His aides made clear that the president intended these suits to have a chilling effect on negative coverage.

One of the instigators of the swimming pool discussion has been Bill Pulte, the director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, according to two people familiar with the discussions. Mr. Pulte has no formal role in White House operations. But he created a foam board rendering of the briefing room restored as an in-ground pool, the people said.

Mr. Pulte often spends his weekends with Mr. Trump at his golf clubs. The president has only a tiny staff around him on the weekends, which means Mr. Pulte often enjoys freewheeling access to Mr. Trump, which he uses to pitch the president on his latest ideas. Senior White House officials say that Mr. Pulte brings along foam boards that highlight potential targets for revenge prosecutions.

Mr. Pulte did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment.

Another top adviser feeding into Mr. Trump’s anti-media tendencies is Boris Epshteyn, the president’s longtime lawyer and outside adviser, who pushed several of the lawsuits the president has filed against news outlets or individual journalists. Mr. Epshteyn’s influence has grown in recent months, according to current officials and people close to the president. Mr. Epshteyn declined to comment.

In September, Mr. Trump startled some of his own advisers by declaring on social media that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House over coverage he called “fiction and lies.” The administration swiftly revoked the credentials of more than 70 journalists.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Natalie Harp, the aide who controls much of the media and messages from supporters that reach the president’s desk, and the majority of his social media feed, had played Mr. Trump clips of MS NOW anchors criticizing his administration shortly before he announced the ban on the three outlets.

Ms. Harp did not respond to a request for comment.

White House officials say the group that provides Mr. Trump updates about news coverage is wider than just Ms. Harp, and that she didn’t intend to prompt the media ban by showing him clips. He made a decision after months of his own anger over coverage, they said. Mr. Cheung singled out Ms. Harp for praise.

Judge Timothy J. Kelly, whom Mr. Trump appointed in his first term, had put a hold on the president’s media ban, saying officials there had violated standard process. But the White House continued for a short period to bar those outlets from the grounds. Judge Kelly last week ruled that the president had violated the outlets’ First Amendment rights and ordered their passes restored. The administration is appealing his ruling.

The campaign against the news media has not stopped there. On Oct. 9, the Justice Department sent letters demanding information from ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News after the five networks temporarily halted their pooled White House TV coverage in solidarity with CNN. People with knowledge of the effort said it was an antitrust investigation.

That Justice Department effort came just a few months after F.B.I. agents showed up at the homes of Times reporters to serve them grand jury subpoenas. Earlier that week, they had reported on security concerns about Mr. Trump while he traveled to Turkey for the NATO summit, as well as the lack of some defensive equipment on the luxury jet, donated by Qatar, that Mr. Trump was using as his new Air Force One.

The president was livid about the reporting and demanded his aides find the leaks, multiple people familiar with the matter said.

The Justice Department withdrew the subpoenas within a few weeks, after the judge in the case admonished federal lawyers for violations of process in appearing to use subpoenas as a first option instead of a last resort to obtain information.

With Mr. Trump’s encouragement, other government departments have taken draconian measures against the press as well. Earlier this year, the Defense Department required credentialed reporters to sign a pledge that included not soliciting unauthorized information. Nearly every major news organization, including Fox News, refused to do so, and instead chose to give up work space in the building.

item.title: Trump Says He Asked Putin to Release an American Jailed in Russia
item.description:
President Trump said on Tuesday that he had asked President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to release Stephen James Hubbard, a Michigan teacher who was seized from his home in Ukraine months after Russia invaded that country in February 2022.

The United States has maintained that the charges against Mr. Hubbard are fabricated. Accused of being a mercenary, he was sentenced to more than six years in a penal colony.

“I’ve been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I’ve been talking to him at length. I’ve asked him to release him. Let’s see what happens.”

He added, “It’s time to have Mr. Hubbard back.”

The return of Mr. Hubbard would allow Mr. Trump to claim a victory for his “America First” foreign policy as he faces mounting blowback, including some from his own party, in his push to rehabilitate Russia on the world stage. Mr. Trump’s courting of Mr. Putin has threated to upend the balance of power in the Ukraine war, alarming both Kyiv and U.S. allies.

Mr. Hubbard, a world traveler, has become an unlikely pawn in that war. The State Department has declared that Mr. Hubbard, 74, was “wrongfully detained,” and former Ukrainian prisoners of war held with him say they believe he will die behind bars if he is not freed.

Mr. Putin has not publicly commented on Mr. Hubbard’s case.

Mr. Trump’s talk of freeing Mr. Hubbard comes as the American president is pushing Ukraine to agree to terms to end Russia’s invasion. He has leveled increasingly harsh criticism at President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has resisted turning over his country’s land and rewarding Russian aggression.

Facing political backlash against high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, the American president has cut a deal to purchase diesel from Moscow and has been promoting it as evidence he is working to lower costs. And he has begun blaming Mr. Zelensky for high diesel prices in the United States.

“Look, we have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine. We’ve got nothing back, other than high diesel,” Mr. Trump said on Tuesday. He added: “We’ve got nothing back, and the American taxpayers are tired of it. We want Zelensky to make a deal.”

In recent months, Mr. Trump’s main envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, have asked Mr. Zelensky not to strike Russian oil refineries. Mr. Zelensky has said he paused refinery strikes for three days to comply with Mr. Trump’s request, but was resuming them.

This week, Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are expected to fly to St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet Mr. Putin in his hometown. There, they are expected to try to secure Mr. Hubbard’s release.

item.title: She Braved Sharks and Storms to Swim the Length of California
item.description:
Catherine Breed was in the Pacific Ocean near San Diego, about three days away from becoming the first person ever to swim the entire California coastline, when the captain of her support boat spotted a mako shark roughly 100 yards away.

Mako sharks are considered the fastest sharks in the ocean. But what would have been a terrifying moment for most people hardly fazed Ms. Breed, an endurance athlete who had already encountered hundreds of other sea creatures, powerful storms and unpredictable currents since her ocean odyssey began at the California-Oregon border on July 1.

Ms. Breed called the shark sightings “a small part of the journey.” Still, her crew took no chances. “I think within like 10 seconds of me seeing the shark, she was on the boat,” said the captain, Maisie Bristow.

Ms. Breed completed the roughly 890-mile voyage on Monday morning, stopping about two miles offshore from Tijuana at the California-Mexico border. She celebrated her historic feat with a small group of friends and crew members aboard the 52-foot sailboat that has been her floating home throughout the expedition, called Swim California.

“It feels surreal being done, this has been my entire life for nearly four months,” Ms. Breed said in a text message shortly after finishing.

The entire expedition took over 100 days, with scheduled rest days and dangerous weather keeping Ms. Breed out of the water for 18 of those days. She averaged more than nine miles on the days that she swam.

“She is an incredible athlete with just incredible mental determination,” said Quinn Fitzgerald, the executive director of the World Open Water Swimming Association, or WOWSA, which is ratifying Ms. Breed’s swim. “But with something as ambitious as this in dynamic and unpredictable water, in an El Niño year, it was not a foregone conclusion despite her talent.”

Born and raised in the Bay Area, Ms. Breed has had a passion for swimming since she was young and eventually received a scholarship to swim at the University of California, Berkeley, where she was a pre-med major, a two-time all-American swimmer and a member of the U.S. national swim team.

After completing several marathon swims across the English Channel, around Manhattan and elsewhere, she turned her sights on the California coastline.

“I’m getting to experience parts of the coast that have never been experienced in this way before. No one goes slowly down the California coast,” she told The New York Times in June, before her journey began.

Ms. Breed encountered a wide range of conditions during the swim. Near the north coast of California, she swam in water that was 48 degrees Fahrenheit, shivering badly on the coldest days when she got back on the boat after hours in the water. Near the end of the swim, the water reached a balmy 75 degrees, though Ms. Breed still wore a wet suit for sun protection and took a course of antibiotics to protect against water polluted with sewage.

About a week before reaching the finish line, Hurricane Rachel swept toward Dana Point in Southern California while Ms. Breed was in the water. The wind rose rapidly in a matter of minutes, she recalled.

“The storm came really fast and many hours early, and so we had to call it,” she said. The boat made it safely back to shore, and Ms. Breed rested the day the hurricane hit. She was back in the water the next day.

But perhaps the greatest challenge was the strong and unpredictable ocean currents, in part because of the intense El Niño conditions this year. Only 19 days into the swim, off Cape Mendocino in Northern California, Ms. Breed’s pace slowed to barely 1 mile per hour — compared with her typical 2 to 3 m.p.h. — as she fought a strong current traveling north.

Having already encountered other powerful currents, she and the crew realized that proceeding at a slower pace could double the length of the expedition, making it impossible to finish before winter with their budget and supplies.

Rather than abandon the swim, the team devised a workaround: Ms. Breed reversed course on sections of the swim where there were powerful currents moving against her. Her support boat would take her south from the previous end point, and then Ms. Breed would swim north to that point. This way she still swam every bit of the distance, just not always in the same direction.

Mr. Fitzgerald says this tactic has precedent. In 2025, when the British athlete Ross Edgley swam around Iceland, he also reversed course for some portions. A WOWSA committee decided that reversing directions would not disqualify his swim.

“Ultimately, it was a safety consideration,” Mr. Fitzgerald said. “We discussed it again for this swim, and the same determination was reached.”

Two of Ms. Breed’s crew members functioned as official observers for the swim. For each half-hour that she was in the water, they recorded her GPS coordinates, as well as photos and video of the swim. A committee from WOWSA will review the logs before ratifying the swim.

Ms. Breed chronicled her journey on Instagram. She also organized and participated in several community events at different locations along the coast to raise awareness about marine conservation issues.

During their time at sea, Ms. Breed and the crew saw hundreds of whales, dolphins and sea lions. They also encountered four great white sharks and pulled her from the water each time.

“There were amazing moments,” Ms. Breed said. “I’ve had a few whales swim with me, dolphins swim with me. Those moments are really special.”

Ms. Breed quit her job at a medical robotics company before starting the expedition, and she’s not sure what she’ll do next. But there’s one thing she’s especially looking forward to: not having to eat so many calories every day.

“I have had to constantly be eating. I eat in the morning. I eat during my swim. I eat right when I get out,” she said. “I’m actually really looking forward to eating for joy again.”

item.title: Mailers About Transgender Students Mysteriously Appear at Texas Homes
item.description:
Just two weeks from Election Day, mysterious messages addressed to transgender children have made their way into Texas voters’ inboxes.

The letters — and text messages — purport to contain help for transgender children preparing for the start of the school year.

The messages includes information about a trans advocacy group — the Transgender Education Network of Texas, or TENT — but the group said it had nothing to do with the messages and the actual origin of the mailers is uncertain.

According to the return address on the letters, the pamphlets were sent by the Texas Transgender Student Union, from an address in an office park area in Meadows Place, outside Houston. But there is no such business registered in Texas, state filings show.

The group appears to be a limited liability company that was created in September in Wyoming, which doesn’t require businesses to disclose who created them.

Transgender rights have been central to this year’s elections in Texas, and the messages caught fire on social media among conservative influencers who received the texts and mailers, which were addressed to “the students” of the family.

“You don’t have to decide about hormones or surgery right now,” reads a pamphlet inside the letter, which includes links to the websites of transgender and civil rights groups. “You don’t have to convince your parents.”

TENT said it did not send the messages and the information within did not represent its official position.

“These text messages and mailers were not authored, authorized, approved, or distributed by TENT and are not affiliated with our organization,” the group said in a statement posted to its website.

Top Republican candidates, including Ken Paxton in the race for U.S. Senate, have made their Democratic opponents’s stances on transgender children in particular a key point of attack.

Voters in Texas, during its most competitive election year in decades, have been inundated by political ads in recent months. Early voting in the Texas election began Monday.

item.title: In Texas’ Senate Race, Paxton and Talarico Converge on Key Battleground
item.description:
For a fleeting moment Monday night, James Talarico and Ken Paxton were perhaps as close as they ever will be physically in their fight for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas.

They were in the same city (Fort Worth), at least, on the same day (the first day of early voting in Texas), delivering speeches at almost the same evening hour, an inadvertent alignment of two campaign tours engaged in a dash to Election Day.

It was no coincidence that they chose Tarrant County for their rallies on the day that voters began casting ballots across Texas. Fort Worth and its surrounding suburbs have become a crucial political battleground. For Republicans in Texas, the contest — for Tarrant County, and therefore Texas, and, Republicans would argue, the future of conservative America — has increasingly been framed as existential.

“This isn’t red versus blue,” Mr. Paxton said to a crowd of more than 200 people seated, along with dozens along a wall, as part of a speech he’s honed for weeks. “It’s the America our founders gave us versus something they would never recognize.”

“Fort Worth, you are my slingshot,” Mr. Talarico told his crowd of more than 1,000 supporters who packed a high school gymnasium, likening them to the biblical David in his successful clash with the more powerful Goliath.

Democrats will likely need to carry the area handily if they are to win the U.S. Senate race. Republicans are eager to hold onto the county, the last large urban area they control in Texas.

Republicans were shaken earlier this year when a Democratic union machinist, Taylor Rehmet, won a special election for a State Senate seat in what had been a solidly Republican area of the county.

Tarrant County has long been a battleground, favoring President Trump in 2016, narrowly backing the Democratic congressman Beto O’Rourke in 2018 for U.S. Senate and Joseph R. Biden Jr. in 2020 before supporting Mr. Trump once again in 2024. But Mr. Rehmet’s win suggested that Democrats were making inroads into the suburbs, and prompted some apparent campaign changes.

“My opponent has done a complete 180, co-opted some of my messaging about working families,” Mr. Rehmet, now a state senator running for re-election, said in an interview from his campaign office. “She even changed the color of her signs to blue.”

That opponent, Leigh Wambsganss, no longer has a photo of Mr. Trump on her website and is no longer referring to herself as “ultra MAGA.”

Blue lawn signs were visible all around Tarrant County this week, including those supporting Ms. Wambsganss, Gov. Greg Abbott and the county’s top executive, Tim O’Hare.

“I don’t think Taylor Rehmet owns a patent on the hottest political topic of the year or the color blue,” Ms. Wambsganss said, referring to the affordability issue. (Mr. Rehmet’s signs are mostly orange.)

On Monday evening, Mr. Paxton, who has appeared with Mr. Trump repeatedly during the president’s recent visits to Texas, motored into Fort Worth in his dark blue and red campaign bus, the words “Endorsed by Trump” written on the back.

Mr. Paxton basked in the rapturous applause of conservatives under the soaring ceilings and Art Deco chandeliers of a former train station waiting room. A full bar served free drinks. Among those cheering were a few supporters of the Make America Healthy Again movement who had come for the opening act: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Mr. Kennedy, who said he could not officially offer an endorsement, instead provided a unique sort of praise for the way Mr. Paxton used his power as the Texas attorney general.

“He was willing to use that power with the same kind of recklessness that President Donald Trump has,” Mr. Kennedy said, in order to “challenge official orthodoxies and vested interests.”

Also praising Mr. Paxton, and issuing warnings about Mr. Talarico, were hard-right figures like the state comptroller, Don Huffines — “We’ve never run against the Communist Party before,” he said — and the conservative commentator Sara Gonzales.

“Are you too dumb to see James Talarico for who he is?” Ms. Gonzales asked.

“No!” the crowd shouted back.

Mr. Paxton read his speech from a teleprompter in a low-key tone, rarely raising his voice. He promised an assortment of tax breaks to address the rising cost of living, compared Mr. Talarico to Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and warned that a vote for Mr. Talarico would be “a vote for Chuck Schumer,” the Democratic senator and minority leader from New York.

“When Republicans vote, we win,” he said, standing at a lectern emblazoned with the words “Ken Paxton Goes After Them.”

Kent Hagood, a 71-year-old with a flowing white beard who works as a Santa Claus during the holidays, liked what he heard.

“I’m hopeful that the polls undervalue the Republican vote,” he said, adding that he was “an example of that” because he does not agree to participate in polls when contacted.

About a 15-minute drive across Cowtown, in southern Fort Worth, Mr. Talarico, who also used a teleprompter, struck a tone that was less “us versus them” than “we’re all in this together” — except for “the billionaires,” who he said had “rigged” the system with the help of politicians like Mr. Paxton.

“This election shouldn’t be about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party. It’s bigger than that,” Mr. Talarico said, echoing a bipartisan message he has deployed throughout his career as a state legislator. “This election should be about chasing a vision of what our state can be.”

He also borrowed a line from the popular Texas high school football drama “Friday Night Lights.”

“As every Texan knows,” Mr. Talarico said, putting himself in the position of the show’s coach. “Clear eyes, full hearts.”

The crowd shouted back, as if players on the fictional team: “Can’t lose!”

More than 1,000 of Mr. Talarico’s supporters sat on bleachers in the gym of North Crowley High School, where there was, as might be expected, no bar. But the crowd still buzzed with a sense of excitement that Mr. Talarico could wrest control of Tarrant County away from Republicans and maybe even deliver the state for Democrats, something that hasn’t happened in three decades.

“I’m hopeful,” Jessica Romo, 36, who works at a cannabis dispensary in Fort Worth, said. “It’s a big crowd.”

Over the summer, the Tarrant County Commissioners Court, led by Republicans, reduced the number of Election Day polling locations by about a third, removing sites including one at the University of Texas at Arlington. The county leaders said it was a cost-saving measure. Democrats said the move would mostly affect Black and Hispanic neighborhoods, which have favored the party.

But some predicted the decision would backfire.

“He’s really energized the base,” said State Representative Ramon Romero Jr., a Fort Worth Democrat, referring to Mr. O’Hare, the Republican Tarrant County executive. “They know that this is a clear attack.”

Addressing the Talarico rally, Alisa Simmons, a Democratic county commissioner who is running against Mr. O’Hare, said she saw positive signs in the large early voter turnout in Tarrant County.

“When we organize, we win,” Ms. Simmons said, “and Tarrant County is proving it right now.”

Those who spoke before Mr. Talarico were all Democrats running for office, except for Todd Smith, a former Republican member of the Texas House of Representatives. Mr. Smith said that one reason for his support for Mr. Talarico was his faith. Mr. Talarico, who has studied at a seminary in Austin, has made his progressive Christianity a centerpiece of his campaign.

“James Talarico has a deep and informed and sincere faith,” Mr. Smith said, “which ensures a value system that will not allow him to lie and cheat and steal.”

Across town, at the Paxton rally, Republicans dismissed and attacked that faith, repeating several times a quote from Mr. Talarico that he saw himself as “a Christian who hates Christianity.” (Mr. Talarico, in the same podcast conversation, had expressed admiration for Jesus’s teachings and opposition to the use of theology to support conservative Republican ideas.)

“How many people do you even know who are Christians and say they hate Christianity?” Mr. Paxton asked.

“None!” one person called out.

item.title: Michigan Senate Candidates Make Dueling Pitches to Business Leaders in Detroit
item.description:
Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, argued on Tuesday that lower taxes and energy bills would make the state more attractive to businesses. About 25 minutes later, on the same stage in Detroit, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate, maintained that the concentration of power in large corporations was driving economic problems.

In dueling appearances, Mr. Rogers and Dr. El-Sayed defended their economic policies before members of the business community, detailing how they would legislate were they to emerge victorious in one of the closest and most hostile Senate races in the country. Each went onstage separately and had an equal amount of time to answer the same set of questions at the Detroit Economic Club, which has hosted interviews with Michigan Senate candidates over the past decade.

Here’s how the candidates, who are scheduled to debate each other on Wednesday night, discussed the topics chosen by the moderator.

Mr. Rogers maintained that Michigan should become more attractive to businesses by improving education so workers could fill available jobs. He cited manufacturing job losses, rising costs and weak literacy as problems that undermined the state’s work force and economy.

Dr. El-Sayed argued that the power imbalance among large corporations was limiting competition, placing consumers, workers and new businesses at a disadvantage. He called for stronger antitrust enforcement and more support for small businesses.

Mr. Rogers said he supported tariffs that would encourage production in the United States, but opposed those he thought harmed Michigan. He cited vehicle production returning to the United States as a benefit, while again distancing himself from President Trump’s trade war with Canada, criticizing those tariffs because many auto parts and vehicles are sold across the border from Michigan.

“If it’s good for Michigan, I’m going to be for it,” Mr. Rogers said. “If it’s bad for Michigan, I’m going to be against it.”

Dr. El-Sayed said he supported some tariffs, but wanted them tied to a longer-term industrial plan rather than applied broadly or unpredictably. He proposed using temporary subsidies and tariffs to help develop a lower-cost electric vehicle built in the United States — a vehicle with a 300-mile range that could cost around $25,000 — and then compete in the global market.

Mr. Rogers argued that being more transparent about prescription drug prices and insurance denial rates could put pressure on providers and help address costs.

Dr. El-Sayed argued for the single-payer health care system “Medicare for all,” framing universal health insurance coverage as an issue for both employees and employers. He said such a system could reduce small businesses’ administrative and cost burdens, and that it could be funded by taxing billionaires’ wealth. He acknowledged that passing “Medicare for all” would require Democrats to be in control of Congress and in the White House.

“Guaranteeing health insurance to everybody in this country would be the single most important thing we could do for small business,” Dr. El-Sayed said.

Mr. Rogers argued that dwindling manufacturing jobs in Michigan had caused wages to fall, and that restoring higher-wage manufacturing work, especially in the defense industry, could help reverse that trend.

Dr. El-Sayed called for more unions, which could push for better wages and benefits, and proposed cutting the employer-side payroll tax so businesses would have more incentive to hire people as artificial intelligence affects the labor market.

Mr. Rogers, who has warned that A.I. presents a national threat, said he supported safety guardrails, including a national-security framework. He also proposed a narrowly limited antitrust exemption that would allow A.I. companies to share information about safety risks. He described the goal as enabling companies to warn one another about dangers.

Dr. El-Sayed is the only Democrat running in a battleground Senate race who has publicly called for a pause on A.I. development or outlined a comprehensive policy program to regulate it. He called on Tuesday for stronger public oversight, citing risks to jobs, human control and communities affected by data centers. He proposed an agency with a role similar to the Securities and Exchange Commission or the Food and Drug Administration to oversee A.I. development.

Mr. Rogers closed with a denunciation of democratic socialism.

“I’ll be damned if I’m going let Detroit become a democratic socialist city,” he said. “It doesn’t work. That’s what’s on the ballot. They’re talking about big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal.”

Dr. El-Sayed appeared to respond, saying that he supported capitalism.

“As I’ve been very clear about, I am a capitalist, but I do not believe we live in actual capitalism,” he said. He added that he supported making the economy more competitive, instead of allowing a few large corporations to dominate the economy — a central pillar of his platform.

“We need to actually start standing up to monopolies and oligopolies and start regulating them, so we can get back to a system where there is competitiveness in a market,” he said.

item.title: Trump’s Super PAC Unleashes Deluge of Ads on Facebook and Instagram
item.description:
President Trump’s political operation has rolled out a major get-out-the-vote program online in the final days of this year’s midterm elections, flooding Facebook and Instagram with ads encouraging Republicans in a number of states to cast their ballots.

Mr. Trump’s super PAC has emerged as the single largest spender nationwide on the two giant social media platforms in recent days, spending more than $1.1. million on Saturday alone. That’s four times as much as the next largest political advertiser that day.

The deluge of digital ads comes as Mr. Trump’s team is trying to boost Republican enthusiasm in the face of the president’s historically low approval ratings. With just two weeks until the midterm elections, polling shows that the president’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries — have threatened the party’s fortunes across the country.

Notably, Mr. Trump’s political operation is aiming its advertising not only broadly at particular states or congressional districts, but specifically at “custom audiences” of individual voters who it hopes are receptive to being pushed to the polls.

A public database of online advertising maintained by Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, shows that 100 percent of the ad spending from Mr. Trump’s super PAC is targeting these custom audiences, which the Trump team provided to the platform.

The ads are running in more than 20 states.

Mr. Trump’s super PAC, called MAGA Inc., has sharply escalated its advertising activity in recent days. The super PAC spent $431,458 on Oct. 14, then $681,107 on Oct. 15, then $822,586 on Oct. 16 and $1,154,832 on Oct. 17, the most recent date for which numbers are available.

The super PAC has run more than 2,200 unique ads just in the last week. Political groups often run large numbers of different ads that can vary in minor ways, to see which are most effective.

Some of the most-viewed ads urge Republicans to vote early. “Beat the lines” and “Do your part,” urge ads running in Michigan, Ohio and Texas that have each been seen more than one million times. Another says, “Don’t turn back the clock,” urging Texans to vote early and declaring that “Democrats broke the border.”

Sagging Republican enthusiasm is one of the party’s key challenges in the final campaign stretch. Many of the tightest contests this year — for both Senate and House — are in more traditionally conservative territory, where Mr. Trump’s political operation hopes to remind voters that there is a consequential election. Operatives are trying to reach particularly those who are likely to vote Republican if they show up.

Also on Tuesday, Mr. Trump began publishing posts on Truth Social urging voters in specific states to vote.

“Early Voting, in-person, is UNDERWAY NOW in the Great State of Maine,” Mr. Trump wrote in one post, with similar messages for residents of North Carolina, Ohio and Iowa, all of which have key Senate contests.

And his super PAC is urging Republicans to head to the polls immediately. Banking votes is a common strategy to help political parties focus their resources more narrowly on those who have not yet cast ballots.

One ad features a photo of Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the two Democratic leaders.

“They’re counting on you to stay home,” reads the ad, with a picture of a hand holding a ballot with red text that reads, “Prove them wrong.”

MAGA Inc. is paying for the ads, but they but they appear online as part of a new Facebook account called Common Sense Voters Coalition.

MAGA Inc. has also begun advertising on Google in recent days for the first time this year, spending $733,000 so far, company records show.

The ads include encouragements such as “Don’t Stay Home,” “Do Your Part,” “Vote Early” and “Make a Plan.”

A spokesman for Mr. Trump’s super PAC declined to comment on the online campaign.

The new digital spending is just one piece of an advertising blitz by the Trump operation since the beginning of September. His allied super PACs have spent nearly $200 million, mostly on television ads, since Sept. 1, according to data from the media-tracking firm AdImpact. Mr. Trump’s team has advertised in Senate and House races in two dozen states, helping give the Republican Party an edge in spending.

Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he planned for the operation to spend more than $400 million in all this cycle. New filings on Tuesday evening will show how much he spent in September.

The spending from MAGA Inc. is not the only get-out-the-vote digital operation on the right.

America PAC, which is funded by Elon Musk, the multibillionaire tech titan, has also been running ads online encouraging people to vote.

On Saturday, the most recent day in the ad database, MAGA Inc.’s spending was more than four times as large as the next closest political advertiser in the country. Next on the list was WinSenate, an offshoot of the top Democratic super PAC focused on Senate races, which spent $289,520 on Saturday.
