item.title: A Billionaire Wanted a Trump Pardon. His Family Gave Alina Habba a $50 Million Deal.
item.description:
Julio Herrera Velutini really wanted a pardon.

A billionaire banker from a prominent Venezuelan family, Mr. Herrera faced felony bribery charges in the United States and struck an unusually lenient plea deal in August 2025 for a misdemeanor campaign finance violation. But he felt that reduced charge was still a stain on his record.

So Mr. Herrera deployed his lawyer, Christopher M. Kise, the former Florida solicitor general who was on Mr. Trump’s personal legal team, to help with a plea for clemency. His 27-year-old daughter, Isabela Herrera, who is an American citizen, donated $3.5 million to a super PAC tied to Mr. Trump. But as of last fall, the pardon remained elusive.

Then the Herrera family hired Alina Habba, who had been one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers and at the time was an adviser at the Justice Department. They offered her $10 million a year for four years along with a range of bonuses. In total, including bonuses, she was guaranteed more than $50 million over four years, according to interviews and documents obtained by The New York Times.

Under the agreement, Ms. Habba would become general counsel at Concord Partners, a company that Ms. Herrera set up in late October 2025 in Florida. The company has no public profile and its business remains unclear even to some people associated with the Herrera business empire. Ms. Habba finalized her deal days after the company was registered.

At the time, Ms. Habba was also a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. She had an office at the Justice Department and a protective detail from the U.S. Marshals, a holdover from her time serving as the U.S. attorney in New Jersey.

She formally began her work for Concord Partners on Jan. 1. Weeks later, Mr. Trump granted Mr. Herrera a full and unconditional pardon.

The sequence of events raises questions about how Mr. Herrera secured the pardon and who might have helped him. People familiar with Ms. Habba’s contract said they believed that she was brought in to help with Mr. Herrera’s push for a pardon and expressed surprise at the scale of the compensation.

Ms. Habba denied any role in the pardon.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” she said in a statement.

Ms. Habba was a special government employee at the time, which allows individuals to work for the federal government for up to 130 days and maintain outside employment with conflict-of-interest restrictions.

She declined to discuss her work for Concord.

Ms. Herrera and Mr. Herrera did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did their companies. In a statement, the Justice Department said Ms. Habba did not speak to anyone about a pardon.

A White House official said that Ms. Habba had nothing to do with the pardon and that the administration follows a pardon review process that includes the White House Counsel’s Office and the Justice Department.

In Mr. Trump’s second term, a pardon industry has sprouted up, with wealthy criminals paying well-connected lawyers, fixers and lobbyists to appeal to the administration and its allies in an effort to secure pardons. Many pardon seekers have come to the conclusion that supporting Mr. Trump and his political agenda is the fastest way to secure clemency.

Some people looking for pardons have reported paying hundreds of thousands of dollars or even $1 million to hire people promising access to the president or influence over the pardon process.

For Ms. Habba, the job from the Herrera family came at a pivotal point in her life and career.

She resigned in December 2025 as U.S. attorney in New Jersey after a panel of federal judges ruled that her appointment by Mr. Trump had been carried out unlawfully. Her second marriage was also falling apart.

The arrangement with the Herreras provided her with a new level of financial security. She also found new love. Shortly after the pardon was issued, Ms. Habba started dating Turhan Mildon, a Turkish investor.

They were married last month in a lavish ceremony in New York. The guest list included Attorney General Todd Blanche; the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel; and Will Scharf, the White House counsel.

The couple is now engaged in high-profile feud with Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally. Ms. Habba has accused Mr. Grenell of misallocating a donation from her husband to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, which Mr. Grenell was running at the time. Mr. Grenell has denied her accusations, calling them absurd.

Ms. Habba brought those accusations directly to Mr. Trump, who directed Mr. Scharf to investigate them. The Times has previously reported that the investigation centers on a bank transfer from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company.

Mr. Herrera, who also has Italian citizenship, is a member of the Herrera family, a banking, real estate and fashion dynasty that dates back to the 14th century. The family owns estates and castles in Caracas, Venezuela; the Canary Islands; Spain; and Germany.

Mr. Herrera founded a bank based in Puerto Rico in 2008.

In August 2022, he was charged for his role in a scheme to bribe Gov. Wanda Vázquez of Puerto Rico to dismiss a regulator who was investigating the bank. Mr. Herrera, Ms. Vázquez and a former F.B.I. agent who had worked as a consultant for Mr. Herrera all pleaded not guilty to felony charges.

Mr. Kise, Mr. Herrera’s lawyer, helped negotiate a deal with the Justice Department under which Mr. Herrera pleaded guilty in August 2025 to a single misdemeanor campaign finance charge. Ms. Vázquez and the former F.B.I. agent also pleaded guilty to misdemeanors, disappointing career prosecutors who had pushed for harsher sentences.

All three were pardoned by Mr. Trump at the same time, shortly before they were scheduled to be sentenced for the misdemeanor charges.

In July, Banvelca, the Herreras’ family office since 1781, announced that Ms. Herrera, a member of the eighth generation and the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, was assuming leadership of the company. Neither the news release nor her bio on the company’s website makes any mention of Concord Partners, the vehicle employing Ms. Habba, who now goes by Mrs. Mildon.

Kenneth P. Vogel contributed to this report.

item.title: A High-Tech Debate in Cattle Country
item.description:
If you want a preview of the country’s political future, look to the exurbs of Denver.

In Colorado’s Eighth District, two millennial candidates competing for a House seat — Representative Gabe Evans, the incumbent Republican, and Manny Rutinel, his Democratic challenger — are having one of the country’s most active debates over the future of A.I.

A.I. has emerged as the Wild West of politics this election cycle, attracting big campaign checks from competing corporate interests and scrambling traditional political lines. Evans and Rutinel, who are running a close race, have both been active in early efforts to regulate the technology.

So last week, while I was in Colorado to report a story on how rising costs are hitting farmers and ranchers, I sat down with both of them to chat about how they’re trying to shape the A.I. future.

To Rutinel, the stakes of the debate are existential.

“This technology has a 10 percent risk of wiping out human civilization,” he told me, in an interview outside a sports bar in Thornton, Colo. “I don’t want human civilization to come to an end.”

Rutinel, who has spent years involved in debates over A.I. regulations and safety, believes government must enact stringent rules dictating how the technology is used.

As a state legislator, he cosponsored a groundbreaking 2024 law that attempted to regulate the use of A.I. by companies and organizations in ways that might be discriminatory. (The law has since been repealed and replaced with a less expansive measure.)

“It’s un-American, it is unpatriotic what’s happening right now. We are just allowing corporate executives to dictate the future of humanity,” he said. “Folks are looking for leaders in this space to make sure that we are putting the right guardrails in place so that we can reap the benefits without the immense catastrophic downsides that are possible.”

What’s surprising is that his arguments for regulation have earned him substantial financial support from the A.I. industry. According to a Times analysis, Rutinel has received more than $240,000 from Anthropic and OpenAI employees, and his campaign has benefited from at least $3 million in spending by PACs with ties to A.I.

Evans, on the other hand, is worried about the consequences of doing too much. Like Trump, he warns that overregulation will allow China to develop A.I. more quickly, leaving the U.S. scrambling to catch up and economically flailing.

“We’ve had these conversations about technology for generations, and when the U.S. leads, you typically have a better outcome,” he told me, in an interview at a different sports bar a couple of miles away. “We have to have common-sense guardrails around this stuff, but you can’t smother it, because if you smother, that doesn’t mean it goes away. It just goes to places like China.”

In August, he introduced legislation directing the Commerce Department to support the adoption and use of American open-source A.I. models over those made by China.

Voters aren’t sure what to make of either of these arguments. Polling from The New York Times and Siena University last month found voters split over which party is better equipped to address A.I.

What is clear is that the issue won’t be going away after the election. And the youngest members of Congress may find themselves leading the conversation in a legislature that’s increasingly geriatric.

Whether it’s Rutinel, 31, or Evans, 40, who wins, the next congressman from the district will be one who came of age in an era defined by rapid technological advancement.

“I’m a millennial,” Evans said, “so I’m not scared of technology.”

Get Caught Up

On Monday, the first day of early voting in Texas, James Talarico and Ken Paxton both held rallies in Fort Worth. For a Senate race with no planned debates, it may be as close as the two candidates ever get.

At a campaign rally in Kansas, Trump invoked a centuries-old antisemitic trope to defend Senator Roger Marshall’s debt-collecting tactics, saying Marshall’s opponents had unfairly cast him as “some kind of a Shylock-type guy.”

Mysterious fliers have started showing up in Texas voters’ mailboxes that purport to offer help for transgender children. A trans advocacy group cited in the mailers says it had nothing to do with them.

Michael Bloomberg, the billionaire former mayor of New York, is giving roughly $80 million to help Democrats in the midterms. He is particularly focused on ensuring a sizable majority in the House.

The Republican National Committee is sending more than $50 million to groups overseeing the party’s efforts to elect House and Senate candidates. The cash infusion is significantly larger than what Republicans have done in the past.

Ad Watch

In Ohio: A new attack ad in the governor’s race features the estranged mother of Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate, accusing her daughter of lying about her past. The two have not spoken since 1978, when Acton, then 12 years old, accused her stepfather of sexual abuse and her mother took the man’s side.

In Michigan: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the Senate, and some Republicans have tried to use that against him, labeling him a “jihadist” and a “Muslim radical.” In a new ad, El-Sayed leans into his identity: “I’m Abdul El-Sayed, man of faith,” he says. “That’s a good thing.”

In Mississippi: Senate Democrats’ main super PAC will air more than $1 million in TV ads in the state. The Senate race there has appeared more competitive in recent weeks, after the Republican incumbent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, said Americans upset about rising beef prices could choose a different protein to eat.

In One Graphic

In this final stretch of the midterms, Republicans are spending a tiny fraction of their total ad buys on ads that mention Trump, according to a Times analysis of data and transcripts from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The total is less than $1 of every $100 spent on ads for House and Senate races from Sept. 9 through Oct. 17. By comparison, Democrats are putting $20 of every $100 in ad spending into spots that mention Trump.

The president has a habit of complimenting men’s appearances at his rallies, often praising the strength and looks of athletes and service members. But he has been especially effusive about Republican candidates on his recent campaign tour. A few examples:

Jon Husted: “He’s got a jawline,” Trump said of Husted, the Senate candidate in Ohio who played college football. Trump said he had carefully examined Husted’s physique — including his hands, his shoulders and his rear — adding, “I never did that with a man before.”

Ed Gallrein: Trump recalled meeting Gallrein, a House candidate in Kentucky. “I needed somebody good, and this guy walks through the door,” he said. “I said, look at this beautiful guy.”

Mike Collins: Trump said at a rally in Georgia that Collins, the Senate candidate, “is a good-looking man — and he’s all man.” (By contrast, Trump claimed that Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent, resembled Pee-wee Herman.)

Rick Jackson: At the same Georgia rally, Trump hailed Jackson, the nominee for governor, as “a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy.”

ONE LAST THING

“The other day I was in a Brioni suit and was accused of being MAGA,” a reader wrote to our chief fashion critic, Vanessa Friedman. The reader wanted to know: Could the label he wore really send an inadvertent message about his political leanings?

It might.

Gone are the days, Vanessa writes, when the only way to wear one’s politics was with a campaign button. The Trump administration’s facility with personal branding means that certain styles — Florsheim shoes; the navy suit, red tie, white shirt combo — have become shorthands for the president and his supporters.

It’s not just the words on a garment that might give clues to your own political position, Vanessa writes, but the actual mixing and matching of the garments themselves.

Taylor Robinson and Matt Zdun contributed to this newsletter.

item.title: ICE Says It Didn’t Hit a Biker With a Car. Video Raises Questions.
item.description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Tuesday denied hitting a cyclist with a car in Long Beach, Calif., before detaining him.

But video footage of the moments before the interaction and an account shared publicly by the man’s daughter offer a different story.

Footage obtained by The New York Times shows the moment an S.U.V. driving the wrong way down a one-way street swerves toward an oncoming bicyclist. An officer jumps out, appearing to draw a weapon that is immediately trained on the rider.

The man on the bike, Ricardo Gonzalez, is an American citizen, according to his daughter, Leslie Gonzalez. She has said on social media that her father was struck by the vehicle.

Mr. Gonzalez has worked for the city of Long Beach, according to the mayor, Rex Richardson, who has submitted a complaint to the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, calling for an independent investigation into the agents’ treatment of Mr. Gonzalez and the overall operation.

Mr. Gonzalez had called 911 at one point on Saturday, the mayor also said. He did not have details about how the altercation unfolded, and it was not clear what, if any, interaction Mr. Gonzalez had with ICE agents before the moments shown on video.

Mr. Gonzalez did not respond to requests for an interview, and Ms. Gonzalez, who initially posted about the encounter on Instagram, also declined to comment further, citing concerns about her family’s safety.

After being confronted by agents, Mr. Gonzalez was “tased” and pinned to the ground, his daughter wrote on Instagram.

In the video footage, Mr. Gonzalez can be heard yelling. “You hit me with your car. I’m a U.S. citizen!” he says, using several expletives.

Mr. Gonzalez was later taken to a hospital for his injuries, the Long Beach police said. The police was not involved in immigration enforcement and did not make any arrests at the scene, the department added. It said its officers were called in for backup by ICE, which had reported that vehicles were being vandalized and that a person needed medical attention. The extent of Mr. Gonzalez’s injuries was not clear on Tuesday.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

In its statement, a spokesperson for ICE said the agency had been conducting a targeted operation to arrest a “criminal illegal alien.” The agency did not say whether it thought Mr. Gonzalez was that person. The agency also said its officers had used “the minimum amount of force.”

“ICE did NOT hit an individual on a bike. An individual was arrested after he smashed the mirror of a government vehicle,” the spokesperson wrote.

ICE described the man, whom the spokesperson did not name, as a “rioter.”

The agency said it was investigating charges for “damage to a government vehicle,” the spokesperson wrote, adding that “anti-ICE agitators attempted to impede operations, threaten officers and damage government vehicles despite officers giving lawful commands."

In many previous violent encounters involving ICE, video footage has appeared to contradict accounts by the agency and other federal officials. In January, President Trump and other members of his administration described how Renee Good, a U.S. citizen was killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis that month, had “weaponized her vehicle” against the federal agent who shot her. Video footage from the scene later revealed no evidence that Ms. Good had run over the agent with her car.

In a similar incident later in January, video footage of the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti revealed inconsistencies between those clips and statements from the Trump administration, including Kristi Noem, who was then homeland security secretary.

Also in January, following an ICE shooting of an immigrant in Minnesota, the agency said the man had violently assaulted a federal officer. Video footage that emerged later did not show such an attack.

Sherman Austin, an I.T. engineer who lives in Long Beach, filmed several videos at the scene on Saturday in the Southern California neighborhood. Mr. Austin, who is 43 and founded an ICE tip network on social media in 2017, said he had been in the area with members of Long Beach Rapid Response, a community group that alerts locals about ICE raids. The group was responding to rumors of unmarked vehicles in the area, which they quickly confirmed.

Mr. Austin said he was warning neighbors when he saw a vehicle speed away down a neighborhood street. He followed that car, which led him to Mr. Gonzalez who was, at that point, already pinned to the ground, Mr. Austin said.

In his videos, Mr. Austin also captured footage of a woman being handcuffed by ICE officers and placed into a car.

“That’s my wife, and that’s a U.S. citizen,” a man is seen yelling in one of the videos, using expletives. The identity of the woman was not clear on Tuesday, and Mr. Austin said he did not know what happened to her.

The neighborhood street quickly became chaotic, as people started yelling at ICE agents and asking local police to intervene.

Mr. Richardson, the mayor, has demanded that ICE agents be taken off assignments during any investigation and that the findings be made public.

“People are upset and outraged, and they should be,” the mayor said in a phone call on Monday.

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

item.title: U.S. Begins Disclosing C.I.A. Interview Reports From Scrutiny of Post-9/11 Torture
item.description:
A former C.I.A. station chief who in 2005 pushed to destroy videotapes of terrorism detainees being tortured at a secret overseas prison later told the F.B.I. that he “did not want to leave a mess” for his successor, and viewed himself as “cleaning up multiple loose ends,” newly declassified documents show.

When the destruction of the tapes came to light in 2007, it prompted an uproar and investigations by the Senate Intelligence Committee and the Justice Department. Those inquiries expanded to examine the torture program itself — one of the most disputed aspects of the Bush administration’s response to the Sept. 11 attacks.

The account by the station chief, who appeared to be based in Thailand even though his location and name were redacted, was among 38 pages of F.B.I. interview notes released to The New York Times in response to a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit seeking records from a criminal investigation led by John H. Durham, a prosecutor who scrutinized the program years later.

The interview notes were the first tranche to be released, chipping away at a wall of secrecy around Mr. Durham’s investigative files. The larger trove of F.B.I. interview reports — some 1,900 pages expected to be released in the coming months — could offer crucial insights into the contentious program. Administrations of both parties have fought for years to keep the records hidden.

“There are a lot of unanswered questions about the Durham investigation — why it closed and what it found,” said Daniel Jones, the chief investigator for the Senate Intelligence Committee’s study. “The release of documents is really important.”

Depending on how much is ultimately released, the reports may provide an oral history of the program from the perspective of C.I.A. participants. The most detailed available history — a 525-page executive summary of a study by the Senate Intelligence Committee that otherwise remains classified — relied on documents. C.I.A. defenders sought to discredit it because committee staff members did not conduct interviews.

Mr. Durham’s concurrent investigation explained that omission. Facing potential criminal jeopardy, C.I.A. officials refused interviews with Senate staff members, and Mr. Durham declined to coordinate interviews by notifying the committee when he had finished with a witness who faced no legal jeopardy. Mr. Durham ultimately decided not to charge anyone at the agency.

The New York Times unsuccessfully sued in 2014 for Mr. Durham’s reports and F.B.I. interview records. After Congress revised legal standards for Freedom of Information Act releases in 2016, the paper sued again in 2022.

Judge James E. Boasberg of the Federal District Court for the District of Columbia, who read the Durham reports privately, ruled in 2024 that they could still be withheld. But the litigation has prompted the government to start releasing redacted versions of the F.B.I. interview records.

How much will become public remains unclear. The first installment covered about 100 pages, but 60 were withheld in full, and the pages released were heavily redacted in places. The government is now supposed to produce additional sets every month. The Times may later challenge some redactions and withheld pages.

One newly disclosed report described an F.B.I. interview with Stephen R. Kappes, a former C.I.A. deputy director, who said agency leaders wanted to destroy the tapes for “political” reasons and “did not recall any discussions that the destruction of the videotapes was illegal.”

The Bush administration secretly created the torture program, which it euphemistically called “enhanced interrogation,” to question high-value detainees in secret overseas prisons. Among other tactics, the C.I.A. used a suffocation technique known as waterboarding, shackled detainees in painful stress positions for long periods, stripped them, doused them in water, slammed them into walls and confined them in small boxes.

A secret memo issued by the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel deemed such tactics as lawful under a broad — and disputed — interpretation of the president’s constitutional power as commander in chief. It claimed presidents could override anti-torture laws and treaties.

A C.I.A. official whose identity was redacted later told the F.B.I. that he had discussed the memo with two agency lawyers, the records show. He “noted that the legal opinion was compelling.”

The office later withdrew the memo. An agency inspector general and the Senate found that the C.I.A. had exceeded the approved tactics, including waterboarding more aggressively than it had told the Justice Department it was doing, and using other techniques, such as forced rectal feeding.

In 2005, the C.I.A. destroyed interrogation videotapes even though the Sept. 11 Commission and a court had sought evidence of questioning sessions. Agency officials later said they feared that the videos would become public, endangering agency personnel whose faces were shown in them.

The newly disclosed files also showed that multiple C.I.A. officials were incredulous that the torture sessions had been videotaped. One official involved, whose name was redacted, questioned whether it was because “executives wanted to know if we were doing it right.”

The agency later shuttered the program and transferred the remaining detainees from its so-called black sites to the military’s wartime prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. Attempted prosecutions before a military commission of several of the detainees, including those accused of helping plan the Sept. 11 attacks, have been impeded by their treatment in C.I.A. custody. A military judge has thrown out their confessions, ruling that they were tainted by coercion.

Michael Mukasey, the Bush administration’s final attorney general, appointed Mr. Durham in 2008 to investigate the C.I.A.’s destruction of the tapes. In 2009, President Barack Obama’s first attorney general, Eric H. Holder Jr., expanded Mr. Durham’s mandate to examine whether the C.I.A. broke laws by exceeding what the Justice Department had approved in its withdrawn memo.

In a terse announcement, the Justice Department disclosed in 2010 that Mr. Durham had decided not to charge anyone over the tape destruction. In 2012, the department said that no one would be charged over detainee treatment, including of two prisoners who died in agency custody. By then, the Senate report was nearly final, though its summary was not made public until 2014.

item.title: Ahead of Midterms, Justice Kagan Says Rulings Have Intensified Polarization
item.description:
Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday criticized the Supreme Court’s conservative majority for a series of election-related decisions in recent years that she said have led to more polarization and a dysfunctional democracy.

Justice Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, delivered the sharp critique two weeks before hotly contested midterm elections and in front of an ideologically mixed crowd of law students and professors. In a wide-ranging discussion, she pointed to the court’s rulings that have loosened restrictions on campaign funding, cleared the way for partisan voting maps and undermined landmark voting rights protections.

“In all these areas, the court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works” and has created “a democracy that does not work as well as it should.”

The justice’s remarks came during a conversation at Catholic University’s law school with Prof. J. Joel Alicea, who was a law clerk to Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr., a conservative.While Justice Kagan has issued strongly worded dissents in individual election-related cases, her remarks on Tuesday amounted to a global critique of how a series of choices by the court’s majority have affected democracy in the United States. Taken together, she said, the rulings have deepened political divisions and made the country’s electoral system work less well.

Justice Kagan wrote the dissent, for instance, when the court in 2019 closed the door on federal litigation challenging voting maps aimed at achieving political ends. As a result, she said, “both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom” to draw voting maps that advantage either Democrats or Republicans in a way that “is very destructive of our democracy.”

Similarly, she said the court’s decisions to ease campaign finance rules have left loopholes that have allowed a massive infusion of political contributions into elections.

“The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare,” she said. “And they’re right.”

Justice Kagan spoke as the court’s new term has begun and ahead of midterm contests that will determine control of Congress, and could require the Supreme Court to intervene in post-election challenges. Election-related litigation has already been filed across the country, with both political parties anticipating the possibility of voter intimidation and the seizure of ballots.

In the coming months, the justices will also hear arguments in high-profile cases involving the legality of bans on semiautomatic rifles, religious rights and President Trump’s aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration.

Even as the court has moved to the right with the addition of three justices nominated by Mr. Trump, Justice Kagan, a nominee of President Barack Obama, has at times found compromise with her colleagues selected by Republican presidents.

Before joining the bench in 2010, she was the dean of Harvard Law School, where she was known for building coalitions and recruiting conservative faculty members.

On Tuesday, Justice Kagan was the first justice who was nominated by a Democratic president and is a non-Catholic to take part in the annual event sponsored by the Center for the Constitution and the Catholic Intellectual Tradition. She is the fifth justice to participate.

She went over the allotted hour for the event and seemed eager to offer a polite takedown of originalism, the theory embraced by conservative justices that the Constitution should be interpreted based on its public meaning at the time it was adopted.

“They were writing the Constitution for the ages. They were writing the Constitution, knowing that there would be change in the world,” she said.

“The whole project” of originalism, she added, “is kind of misconceived, and it’s not a very good match with the Constitution we have.”

Even as Justice Kagan faulted the conservative majority for not considering the consequences of its election-related rulings, she reiterated her defense of the conservative-dominated bench from a July appearance and said it was a “bum rap” to suggest the court had been too deferential to Mr. Trump.

In the court’s term that wrapped up in late June, the justices delivered long-sought conservative wins that expanded presidential power over immigration and the federal bureaucracy, in addition to dealing a blow to the Voting Rights Act of 1965, a landmark civil rights law.

But the court, including justices nominated by Mr. Trump, also rejected some of his marquee policies. The court struck down the president’s tariffs, blocked his order to end the guarantee of birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born babies of undocumented immigrants and prevented him from immediately firing a leader of the Federal Reserve.

Recent polls have shown declining public opinion of the Supreme Court with a majority of Americans saying the justices are motivated mainly by politics rather than law, according to a September survey conducted by Marquette University Law School. Those unfavorable views come as Democratic officials and candidates are increasingly calling for structural changes to the court should the party win control of Congress.

Justice Kagan said the court she joined 16 years ago was more balanced and held in higher esteem by the public in part because it was less predictable. She pointed to the period after Justice Antonin Scalia died in 2016 when she said the justices had to compromise, listen and issue narrow rulings to try to avoid being deadlocked 4 to 4.

“There was a period of time where the court was in a better place and the country was in a better place because the court was more balanced and it was unclear whether the court could push through anybody’s program.”

“Nobody in America thought that the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party,” she said, “and the court had a kind of legitimacy.”

item.title: Trump Wields an Unprecedented $277 Million in Final Midterm Stretch
item.description:
President Trump’s political operation dedicated about $277 million from September through mid-October to help Republican midterm candidates, a staggering sum that has given the party an upper hand financially as it clings to full control of Congress.

That spending, unheard-of for a term-limited president, is an unbridled expression of Mr. Trump’s power. Immediately upon being elected for the second time, his aides began soliciting checks at dinners where companies and donors angling for influence could buy face time with the leader of the free world, sometimes for a million dollars a head. His main super PAC, MAGA Inc., has raised about $473 million since his election — and now Mr. Trump is putting that money to work.

The money has financed an explosion of Republican spending that Democrats have had no answer for, even as they aim to take advantage of an otherwise favorable political environment.

Around Labor Day, Mr. Trump’s three outside groups started running advertisements in 24 states that included some of the most competitive Senate and House races. Plenty of the seats, notably, were in red areas and have become competitive for Democrats because of Mr. Trump’s unpopularity. In recent days, the Trump-tied super PACs have drastically increased their spending on ads through Meta and Google.

The New York Times previously reported that two of these super PACs were effectively outgrowths of MAGA Inc. And new campaign-finance filings posted on Tuesday evening from those groups, called No Going Back PAC Inc. and Safety and Affordability PAC Inc., show that they were almost entirely financed with $225 million in transfers from MAGA Inc. through Oct. 14.

Mr. Trump’s three allied super PACs together held about $181 million on hand as of Oct. 14, the filings showed, meaning that they could spend heavily to help Republicans over the final three weeks.

Between Oct. 15 and Election Day, those three affiliated super PACs are slated to air roughly $99 million worth of ads, according to the media-tracking firm AdImpact. That most likely puts the Trump operation’s total spending for the midterms above $300 million.

Mr. Trump — who some Republicans had doubted would direct his super PAC to spend this much on the midterms — proudly pointed on Tuesday afternoon to the money from his operation.

“I have spent, or will be spending, over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day,” he wrote on Truth Social. “More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more.” (He seemed to be suggesting that the groups’ money was his, a claim that has raised legal scrutiny.)

The biggest donors to Mr. Trump’s main super PAC since Election Day in 2024 have been the crypto company Foris Dax, which operates Crypto.com; the Wisconsin roofing billionaire Diane Hendricks; and the pro-Israel megadonor Miriam Adelson, according to a New York Times review of MAGA Inc. records.

But the operation has raised money from a wide group of donors, some of whom have business before the Trump administration. Over 100 contributors have given at least $1 million to MAGA Inc., according to the Times review.

Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting.

item.title: New Video Shows Chaotic Moments Before Mississippi Police Shot Toddler
item.description:
Moments before a Mississippi police officer fired at a car this summer, killing a toddler inside, five officers rushed out to a Walmart parking lot in pursuit of two women who were accused of stealing diapers and baby clothes.

Newly released videos show a gray sedan, carrying 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, his mother and another woman, reversing and slamming into a parked vehicle as police officers run toward the car and order the driver to stop.

As the car stops, the officers approach and surround the vehicle before the driver accelerates and lurches left, appearing to travel toward at least one of the officers before passing between two of them. At least one officer shoots into the vehicle.

The chaotic scene in Senatobia, Miss., captured on body cameras worn by two of the five officers and by surveillance cameras, provides the first glimpse of a shooting that has rocked the tiny city and raised questions about whether the officer was justified in opening fire at the vehicle.

The Mississippi attorney general’s office, which declined to comment on the video, announced on Monday that it would not bring criminal charges against the officer who fatally shot Kohen.

The compilation of several body-cam and surveillance clips was first published by a local news outlet, Darkhorse Press. A law enforcement official confirmed its authenticity on the condition of anonymity because the official was not authorized to provide information about sensitive matters. A video analysis by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News showed the footage matched portions of video of the shooting captured by a bystander.

The body-cam footage released Tuesday is from the perspective of two of the law enforcement officers who responded to the scene in June, but not from the officer who fired. It does not show the entirety of the police response, nor does it clearly show Kohen, his mother and the other woman driving the vehicle.

The body-cam footage begins from the perspective of one of the officers, whose identity is unknown. It shows him rushing toward the gray sedan.

The footage then shows the vehicle move in reverse and hit a parked S.U.V. as officers approach, yelling at the driver to stop. When the sedan moves forward, at least one officer appears to be in front of it on the passenger’s side; a second officer also stands near the vehicle, closer to the driver’s side. Both have their guns drawn. As the vehicle approaches them, at least one of the officers opens fire. The officer appears to fire three more times while standing to the side of the vehicle.

Grainy surveillance footage included in the compilation published by Darkhorse Press also captures the moments from more of a bird’s-eye view. In that footage, two women — one holding a child — are seen running toward a vehicle and reversing in it as law enforcement officers chase them.

More video of the incident has yet to be seen by the public. Kohen’s family is scheduled to view it Thursday morning. Veronica Roberson, the toddler’s grandmother, said state officials had informed the family that the footage included surveillance videos from Walmart, along with five body-worn cameras.

Hunter Foster, an officer with the Senatobia Police Department, was placed on leave while state authorities investigated his actions at the Walmart. Although he has not been named as the one who opened fire, Officer Foster is the only officer among those present that day who was placed on leave.

The shooting death touched off weeks of protests and calls for transparency in Senatobia, a city of roughly 8,400 located roughly 40 miles south of Memphis. Activists and Kohen’s family had been calling on the authorities to release police body-camera or dashcam footage.

Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, said she had been holding her son in her arms in the front passenger seat when the driver, Latoya Ferrell, tried to back out of a space and then drive forward. Ms. Ferrell was seriously injured.

In the hours after the shooting, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation issued a statement saying the police had fired at a vehicle when it drove toward an officer, “almost striking” one.

Jerry Mitchell, Julie Lee, Aric Toler and Alexander Cardia contributed reporting.
